summary: Defines a DHCP option that tells a client the order in which to consult name services, such as DNS or local files, when resolving hostnames and other information.

eli5.summary: When your computer wants to find a name, it can ask several sources. This tells it which to ask first.

questions: how to set name resolution order with dhcp
subtitle: Allows DHCP servers to specify the order for consulting name services

tldr.problem: Many clients use multiple name services (DNS, NIS+, local files) but have no standard way to learn the order in which to consult them; each client crafts its own conventions.
tldr.mechanism: DHCP option 117 carries a list of 16-bit option codes in preferred order, referring to previously-defined DHCP options that specify name service IP addresses, allowing servers to express a consistent search order.
tldr.outcome: Clients can use a DHCP-provided search order rather than relying on local configuration, enabling administrators to coordinate name resolution across a network.

today: RFC 2937 is a Proposed Standard that specifies how DHCP communicates name service search order to clients. It remains published and is used by DHCP servers to coordinate name resolution policies across networks.

sections.title: Name Service Search Order
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) provides a framework for passing configuration information to hosts on a TCP/IP network. RFC 2132 allows DHCP servers to specify configuration information for various name services. Many clients use multiple name services—such as DNS, NIS+, or local files—and need to know the order in which to consult them when resolving hostnames and other information.

Before this RFC, no standard mechanism existed to specify a search order via DHCP. This document enables DHCP servers to communicate the preferred order for consulting various name services, avoiding the need for each client to maintain its own conventions.
sections.eli5: Networks can have several different ways to look up names. This defines how a server can tell a client which method to try first, second, and so on.

sections.title: The Name Service Search Option Format
sections.content:
DHCP option 117 carries a list of 16-bit network byte order (big-endian) integers, each representing the option code for a name service. The server returns these codes in preferred order: earlier codes in the list indicate more preferred name services.

The option has a minimum length of 2 bytes. Example name service option codes include code 6 for Domain Name Servers (DNS), code 41 for Network Information Servers, code 44 for NetBIOS over TCP/IP Name Servers, and code 65 for NIS+ Servers. A code value of 0 indicates that the client should refer to local naming information (such as /etc/hosts on UNIX).
sections.eli5: Each name service has a number. The server lists these numbers in the order the client should try them, with the most important ones first.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content: The DHCP client uses option 117 to create a search list for name resolution. A client may receive name services in this option that it does not support or has not been configured to access. Likewise, a client may receive an option that lists name services for which no corresponding DHCP option was supplied with server IP addresses. Clients interpret this option in a system-specific manner whose specification is outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.eli5: The client follows the order it receives, but how exactly it uses the list depends on the system. It might skip services it doesn't know about.
